sections.heading: 4.1. Dataset Collection and Training
sections.text: As previously stated, producing task-specific variants of Canvas largely centers around collecting training data that matches the desired use case, then fine-tuning the generic base model on this dedicated dataset. In the case of background outpainting, we collect a dataset of in-context product photographs, where a product to be advertised is prominently featured in a real-world scene. We use InSPyReNet ( Kim et al., 2022 ) to obtain these foreground masks. As a preprocessing step, we apply this mask to the input product photograph, removing the original background and replacing it with a plain white background. Then, during training, the model is provided this masked product shot, along with a text caption describing the original image and background, and is supervised to reconstruct the original unmasked image. During inference, after running the diffusion loop and obtaining the final generation, we then additionally composite the original product cutout back onto the generated image. This is a further safeguard to avoid any potential modifications—our use of segmentation masks during training ensures the model won’t extend the product beyond its existing boundaries, and reusing the original product shot ensures the model cannot inadvertently alter the product itself. We also implement dynamic positioning and padding, deriving the vertical placement and padding from the original product shot instead of using a fixed centered layout, to better accommodate product-specific composition. Aspect ratio outpainting follows a similar protocol, though naturally we no longer need to produce segmentation masks for the products themselves. Thus, instead of masking out the background, we mask out bands along the top and bottom of the input images, and the model is trained to reconstruct the original image, thereby “extending” the training sample.

sections.heading: 4.1.1. Outpainting VAE
sections.text: We observe occasional color mismatches, especially in the aspect ratio extension setting, where the boundary between the original image and the newly generated bands along the top and bottom are visibly distinct. To improve color harmonization, we start from the FLUX.1 VAE distilled on Pinterest data and fine-tune the decoder to accept mask and masked image inputs for outpainting tasks. Comparisons between the original FLUX.1 VAE and the fine-tuned outpainting VAE are provided in Appendix C .

sections.heading: 4.1.2. Super-resolution
sections.text: Our base outpainting pipeline generates images at 416 × 608 416\times 608 to improve the efficiency of multiple-generation settings. To meet product high-resolution requirements, we upscale the top-ranked candidate by × 3 \times 3 to 1248 × 1824 1248\times 1824 using a Canvas super-resolution variant, and then composite the original high-resolution product cutout back into the final output. Notably, InSPyReNet segmentation is computed at the original high-resolution original input to better capture the detailed product boundaries.

sections.heading: 4.2.2. Eligibility
sections.text: Background outpainting is suitable for product images with plain white backgrounds, whereas aspect-ratio outpainting is primarily applied to lifestyle images with suboptimal aspect ratios. We therefore perform pre-generation eligibility filtering to focus on inputs that are likely to yield meaningful enhancement. In practice, we filter background outpainting candidates by requiring a white dominant background and no human presence. For aspect-ratio outpainting, we exclude white/solid-color backgrounds and require no human presence and images with a height:width aspect ratio < 1.4 . We additionally exclude cases that are prone to failure modes e.g., out-of-frame products, heavy obstructions, overlays, text-dominant images, or patterned images.

sections.heading: 4.2.3. Human Review
sections.text: Merchants are often reluctant to deploy AI-generated content without reliable quality controls. Although VLMs offer a scalable and low-cost alternative for automated screening, we find that they do not consistently detect subtle defects or enforce strict requirements such as complete product preservation. We therefore design structured human-review templates and rely on trained human raters to identify fine-grained artifacts and ensure that outputs are safe and visually appealing. Each generated image is independently reviewed by two raters following the rubric and template in Appendix D . For background outpainting, raters assess product defect and background defect; for aspect-ratio outpainting, raters assess eligibility and background defects. An output is marked defective if either rater flags any question as defective.

sections.heading: 4.2.4. Multiple-generation and Reward Model
sections.text: In our production pipeline, we use inference time computation to produce multiple generations to increase the likelihood of obtaining an acceptable output. Considering the inference cost, we generate two candidates per input. For background outpainting, diversity is introduced through different prompts, whereas for aspect-ratio outpainting it is introduced through different random seeds. To avoid increasing human-review load, we use a reward model to automatically select the top-ranked candidate to send for rater review. Leveraging large-scale historical rater annotations, we train internal reward models to approximate human judgments. Details of the reward model are in Appendix E .

sections.heading: 4.2.6. Post-generation Filtering
sections.text: In some cases, even the top-ranked candidate receives a low reward score due to predictable failure modes, e.g., segmentation errors, out of frame products, etc. This indicates that the product input is unlikely to pass human review and should be filtered out before review. To address this, we generate a larger batch of candidates, score and rank them with the reward model, and discard the product inputs with severe predicted defects that are likely to fail in subsequent human evaluations, thereby improving the overall yield.

sections.heading: 5.2. Online A/B Results for Outpainting
sections.text: Canvas was deployed in Pinterest Performance+ suite and we conducted A/B tests. For background outpainting, the control group is the original product shot images with a white background and the treatment group swaps white background images with background outpainted images generated by Canvas on Home Feed, Related Pins, and Search. For aspect-ratio outpainting, the control group are original product shot images with a lifestyle background and the treatment group are aspect-ratio outpainted ones. sections.heading: Appendix C Outpainting VAE for Color Harmonization
sections.text: We fine-tune the VAE decoder to take two additional inputs of a mask and a masked image, alongside the outpainted image. This improves color harmonization by blending the inputs across multiple feature scales, particularly for aspect-ratio outpainting where boundary color mismatches can occur. Figure 10 compares decodes from the standard FLUX.1 VAE and our outpainting VAE using the same generated latents, where the FLUX.1 VAE shows a visible background color discontinuity and seam at the boundary (denoted by yellow arrow), while the outpainting VAE produces a smoother blend across the transition.
